Plunged into chaos
The shrinking of USAID threatens numerous health programmes in Africa

Of more than 10,000 employees of the US development cooperation agency, fewer than 300 could remain; health projects would be left without funding and important programmes would have to consider alternatives: a dismantling of USAID would hit the African continent hard.

By Katharina Moser, Windhoek

While US President Donald Trump, in the name of American interests, knocks the basic principles of the powerful country's foreign policy and international cooperation off their hinges, recent weeks have quickly shown who feels the consequences of these decisions most - among them the African continent. After almost the entire staff of the US development agency, the United States Agency for International Development (USAID), was placed on leave on Friday, numerous African countries may be facing the shattered remains of many health programmes whose funding was closely tied to the US agency's programmes. In 2024 alone, the US provided almost 6.6 billion US dollars in humanitarian aid to sub-Saharan Africa.

To the great relief of the opponents of Trump's decisions, a federal judge on Friday dealt Trump and his billionaire ally Elon Musk their first major setback in the dismantling of the US agency for international development, ordering a temporary halt to plans to remove thousands of the agency's employees from duty. This was reported by the Associated Press, among others. US District Judge Carl Nichols, a Trump appointee, also agreed to block an order that would have given the thousands of USAID employees overseas, whom the government wanted to place on abrupt administrative leave, only 30 days to return to the US with their families and households at government expense. The judge also ordered that USAID employees already placed on leave by the Trump administration be reinstated. However, he rejected a request by two federal employee unions to grant a temporary block on the funds frozen by the Trump administration, which has paralysed the six-decade-old agency and its work, until further hearings on the employees' lawsuit take place.

How things will now proceed with the agency is unclear for the time being. Workers have already used a crane to scrub the name from the stone facade of the Washington headquarters, taped over the lettering on a sign and taken down the USAID flags. Now the health sector on the African continent and worldwide is looking anxiously to Washington: should Trump be able to push through the dissolution of the agency, it would have serious consequences for health programmes worldwide.

What would the dissolution of USAID mean?

The loss of USAID could lead in Africa to an interruption of emergency responses to outbreaks such as mpox and the Marburg virus, the magazine Nature reports. Training programmes that have been accelerated since the COVID-19 pandemic could slow down. HIV/AIDS testing, treatment and prevention programmes would be affected, as would immunisation initiatives.

Not least in Namibia, several Namibian health programmes would be left without funding and many of the staff, including nurses, without work (AZ reported). With funds from the President's Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief (PEPFAR), the USAID Global Health Supply Chain Programme - Procurement and Supply Management (GHSC-PSM) supported, not only in Namibia, the government's goals as well as important PEPFAR initiatives under the 2016 Treatment Acceleration Plan (TAP).

"The world will become less safe as a result"

The decisions of the US under Trump - besides the freezing of foreign aid, also its withdrawal from the World Health Organization in Geneva - would affect billions of dollars in annual funding to fight HIV, malaria and other areas of global health, the magazine Nature reports. This will cost lives and threaten global security, researchers say according to the magazine. "The world will become less safe as a result," said Peter Horby, an infectious disease researcher at the University of Oxford, Britain, to the magazine. From 2000 to 2021, USAID's work helped prevent 7.6 million deaths from malaria, according to The Conversation. USAID's work on the development and introduction of the malaria vaccine, which had been seen as a turning point in the fight against the disease, would now also be called into question.

"There is chaos," says an HIV researcher in Africa to Nature, who runs a clinic in which thousands of patients are treated and which is supported by a US programme called the President's Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief (PEPFAR), and who does not wish to be named for fear of reprisals. According to Nature, more than 20 million people, mainly in Africa, including more than a million children and pregnant women, receive antiretroviral medicines under the 6.5 billion US dollar programme. "People had no chance to find alternative sources of funding, because the matter came so suddenly," says Salim Abdool Karim, director of the centre for the AIDS research programme in South Africa in Durban.

The Trump administration did grant an exemption for the continuation of "life-saving humanitarian assistance." This included the programme that gives 20 million people with HIV/AIDS access to antiretroviral medicines. The future of the US AIDS organisation, the President's Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief (PEPFAR), is nevertheless in question, reports Natasha Lindstaedt, professor in the department of government at the University of Essex, in The Conversation.

In South Africa it took only a few days for the effects of US President Donald Trump's numerous executive orders last week to become noticeable. There were already reports of HIV clinics closing, planned training programmes being cancelled and trans health centres closing, journalist Morgan Morris reported in Nature magazine.

Abdool Karim hopes that in South Africa, where the government carries out the bulk of HIV treatment with the help of PEPFAR funds, the effects of the possible dissolution of the agency would be minimal. But in many other African countries "the effects would be catastrophic if PEPFAR services were discontinued. Governments cannot simply step in to close the gap."

Elon Musk was the driving force

According to Trump's original plans, the agency was to be massively wound down starting at the weekend, as Tagesschau reported. Before the court stepped in, the administration of US President Donald Trump wanted to reduce the number of employees from more than 10,000 to just under 300. A union representative confirmed the corresponding figures from US media reports. The broadcaster NPR reported that US Secretary of State Marco Rubio had been presented with a list of around 600 employees whose work worldwide was deemed essential. Rubio, however, exempted fewer than 300 from being placed on leave.

While USAID, as an independent government agency, has since 1961 funded programmes worldwide in the areas of health care, democracy promotion and civil society, Elon Musk called it a "nest of vipers of radical-left Marxists who hate America." The right-wing conservative broadcaster Fox News, which is close to Trump and the Republican Party, claimed that allegations had been come across that the agency had allegedly funded terrorist organisations and Chinese groups. Former USAID employee Mark Moyar claimed on Fox News that the staff had been intent on "undermining the president's will on policy questions" and on sending taxpayer money abroad in order to promote DEI and LGBT initiatives.

Opponents of Trump's policies point out that these corruption allegations largely appear to lack any factual basis. The White House had claimed, for example, that USAID had used more than eight million dollars to support the media organisation Politico. As the Washington Post showed, records prove that only 44,000 USD went from USAID to Politico.

Also harms US interests

"What Trump's team misunderstands is that USAID's work is also indispensable for safeguarding American interests," says Lindstaedt. "China, which since 2013 has invested more than a trillion US dollars in infrastructure projects in Asia, Africa, Europe and Latin America, is now being given the opportunity to exert more influence worldwide. The gap in US aid is a gift to China in the battle for soft power."

Not only would a dissolution of USAID mean the end of life-saving global health programmes, of early warning systems and food security efforts - a gap would also open up into which other countries can step, said Andy Kim, senator from New Jersey, to CNN. "Trump's actions weaken the global leadership role and influence of the US at a time when we are confronted with serious national security threats," said the Democrat. "Trump is opening the door to our competitors and adversaries."

USAID is not only altruistic but also serves national interests, says George Ingram too, a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution and a former USAID official under the Clinton administration, speaking to the broadcaster. The agency can develop markets with which the US can trade, and had also helped make countries more stable, which in turn could curb global migration and prevent the US from being drawn into conflicts overseas. USAID's climate programmes had fought energy poverty but had also created a level playing field for US companies in the field of renewable energy, said Gillian Caldwell, former USAID climate officer, who left the agency at the end of December, speaking to CNN.

For some experts the possible dissolution of USAID is a wake-up call, Nature reports. According to Angela Apeagyei, assistant professor at the Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation (IHME) at the University of Washington (USA) and author of a study on health spending in sub-Saharan African countries in 2024, African countries must ultimately become more independent of external donors and "give priority to domestic financing of the health sector and to efficient management of public finances."

In Namibia, meanwhile, ministry spokesperson Walters Kamaya affirmed that Namibia will continue its health measures despite the loss of US aid. He stressed that USAID funding represents merely a supplementary resource and must also be regarded as such. "With or without USAID, we will continue to provide health services for our people. Of course the loss will be felt, but that cannot be an excuse for failing."

[The article body is repeated verbatim a second time in the source page.]

a6385.t:
By BUUMBA CHIMBULU
A PACT to promote and facilitating a conducive business environment for the private sector has been entered into between Government and the United States Agency for International Development (USAID).
The agreement was signed between the Ministry of Commerce, Trade and Industry, and the USAID Business Enabling Project in Lusaka during the week.
The ministry’s Permanent Secretary for Investment and Industrialisation, Mr Crusivia Hichikumba explained that the agreement was a testament to the shared commitment to creating an ecosystem where businesses could thrive.
Mr Hichikumba, speaking at the signing ceremony, noted that this was also aimed at creating an environment for businesses to innovate, and contribute to the nation’s economic development.
“As you may be aware, the Ministry of Commerce, Trade, and Industry is charged with the responsibility for formulating and implementing policies aimed at creating a conducive business environment for private sector growth,” he said.
Mr Hichikumba said the ministry was dedicated to driving economic progress through strategic collaborations and initiatives that support the private sector.
He said the government recognises that a robust and dynamic private sector is crucial for job creation, innovation, and sustainable economic growth.
Mr Hichikumba however said achieving this required an enabling environment where businesses can operate efficiently, access essential resources, and navigate regulatory frameworks with ease.
“The USAID Business Enabling Project has been a steadfast partner in our journey towards achieving these goals,” he said.
Mr. Hichikumba added that through the agreement, the government was establishing a framework for implementing programmes that would address key challenges faced by our business community.
He said the programmes would focus on streamlining regulatory processes as well as fostering innovation and entrepreneurship.
“This collaboration is also a reflection of our commitment to aligning with international best practices and leveraging global expertise to address local challenges,” he said.
Mr Hichikumba noted that the USAID Business Enabling Project brings a wealth of knowledge and experience that will be invaluable in the government efforts to create a more competitive and inclusive economy.

a6392.t:
Os países mais afectados são a Zâmbia e o Zimbabué, enquanto Moçambique, a Tanzânia, a República Democrática do Congo, a Etiópia e a Nigéria registaram surtos activos de cólera, com um total de 26.000 casos e 700 mortes, segundo a OMS.
"As alterações climáticas e os conflitos estão a alimentar o fogo. Inundações, ciclones e secas reduzem o acesso à água potável e criam um ambiente ideal para o desenvolvimento da cólera", explicou a gestora de emergências do Gabinete Regional da OMS para África, Fiona Braka, por teleconferência a partir de Brazzaville, a capital da República do Congo.
Na Zâmbia, a vacinação contra a cólera começou nas comunidades mais afetadas, com o objectivo de vacinar 1,7 milhões de pessoas, enquanto no Zimbabué a cobertura está prevista para 2,3 milhões de pessoas.
Braka disse que estas campanhas de vacinação representam um esforço importante no qual a OMS está a colaborar, porque as reservas internacionais de vacinas contra a cólera são escassas.
Por isso, considerou também que devem ser analisadas soluções que incluam um melhor acesso a água potável, higiene e instalações sanitárias, bem como um diagnóstico e tratamento de qualidade.
Em Moçambique, segundo o mais recente boletim sobre a progressão da doença, elaborado pela Direção Nacional de Saúde Pública e com dados até 31 de Janeiro, estava contabilizado um acumulado de 10.859 casos de cólera desde 01 de Outubro de 2023.
Relativamente à Etiópia, o Reino Unido anunciou um pacote de ajuda humanitária de 100 milhões de libras (117 milhões de euros). Este programa pretende permitir a mais de três milhões de etíopes, na maioria mulheres e crianças, o acesso a serviços de saúde, nomeadamente para combater a malnutrição e os surtos de malária e de cólera.
A Comissão Europeia também se manifestou relativamente aos surtos de cólera e vai ajudar, com um milhão de euros, a combater a epidemia na Zâmbia, que poderá atingir 3,5 milhões de pessoas.
a6392.en:
Cholera. WHO warns of worsening cases in Eastern and Southern Africa

The most affected countries are Zambia and Zimbabwe, while Mozambique, Tanzania, the Democratic Republic of Congo, Ethiopia and Nigeria have recorded active cholera outbreaks, with a total of 26,000 cases and 700 deaths, according to the WHO.

"Climate change and conflicts are fuelling the fire. Floods, cyclones and droughts reduce access to drinking water and create an ideal environment for cholera to develop," explained the emergency manager of the WHO Regional Office for Africa, Fiona Braka, by teleconference from Brazzaville, the capital of the Republic of the Congo.

In Zambia, cholera vaccination has begun in the most affected communities, with the aim of vaccinating 1.7 million people, while in Zimbabwe coverage is planned for 2.3 million people.

Braka said that these vaccination campaigns represent an important effort in which the WHO is collaborating, because international stocks of cholera vaccines are scarce.

For that reason, she also considered that solutions should be examined that include better access to drinking water, hygiene and sanitation facilities, as well as quality diagnosis and treatment.

In Mozambique, according to the most recent bulletin on the progression of the disease, prepared by the National Directorate of Public Health and with data up to 31 January, a cumulative total of 10,859 cholera cases had been recorded since 1 October 2023.

With regard to Ethiopia, the United Kingdom announced a humanitarian aid package of 100 million pounds (117 million euros). This programme aims to give more than three million Ethiopians, mostly women and children, access to health services, in particular to combat malnutrition and outbreaks of malaria and cholera.

The European Commission has also spoken out regarding the cholera outbreaks and will help, with one million euros, to fight the epidemic in Zambia, which could affect 3.5 million people.

a6620.t:
Malawi’s actual grant disbursements will fall short by 61.8 percent of the target in the 2025/26 financial year following aid cut and US tariff impositions, the African Development Bank (AfDB) has projected
In its 2025 Country Focus published on Monday, the pan-African bank said this has been compounded by the suspension of $350 million annual funding from the United States Agency for International Development (USaid), the cancellation of the $350 million (about K613 billion) five-year Millennium Challenge Corporation (MCC) land compact and the imposition of an 18 percent tariff on exports from Malawi to the US.
Reads the bank’s report in part: “While the first-round trade effects of the tariffs are limited due to the small share of Malawi’s exports to the US at [less than four percent], the aid cuts will have a big effect given that 87 percent of aid is allocated to capital projects, directly affecting infrastructure development and economic growth.
“The second-round trade effects emanate from reduced global growth, especially that of South Africa, the European Union and the United Kingdom, which will reduce Malawi’s export demand.”
AfDB observed that in the medium-to-long-term, both aid cuts and tariff imposition will have employment, productivity and competitiveness and growth effects that will exacerbate macro-fiscal instability.
AfDB data further show that while domestic revenue has risen from 14.7 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) in 2022 to 18.1 percent of GDP in 2024, expenditures have risen from 26.8 percent of GDP in 2022 to 32 percent of GDP in 2024 in the face of rising financing gap of about $3.59 billion (about K6.2 trillion) or $0.63 billion (K1.1 trillion) annually.
This would enable the country to fast-track structural transformation for the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development, which envisions a secure world free of poverty and hunger and the African Union’s Agenda 2063, a blueprint and master plan for sustainable development and economic growth of the continent.
In an interview, Centre for Social Concern economic governance officer Agnes Nyirongo observed that the sharp decline in disbursements has left a substantial funding gap, undermining the government’s ability to meet its obligations.
She said: “Grant financing is predominantly allocated to capital projects such as infrastructure development, healthcare systems, education facilities, agricultural support programs, and public works.
“The loss of this funding means delays or outright cancellation of projects, threatening employment, productivity and service delivery. Many initiatives tied to long-term growth are now hanging in the balance.”
Minister of Finance and Economic Affairs Simplex Chithyola-Banda projected grants at K1.17 trillion in the 2024/25 fiscal year, with K1.1 trillion xpected from international organisations and K72.69 billion from foreign governments.
This means that at 67 percent, grants would have declined by about K800 billion.
Ministry of Finance and Economic Affairs spokesperson Williams Banda was yet to respond to our questionnaire, but is quoted as having said that only K9.2 billion of USAid funding appeared in the 2024/25 National Budget, but that the US government off-budget projection in 2024/25 fiscal year was about K307 billion.
In his earlier comment following the cancellation of MCC, Minister of Transport Jacob Hara said the compact came with funding for ongoing road works.
“We shall have to start from scratch looking for new financing,” he said.
In the MCC compact, $244 million (about K427 billion) was budgeted for the roads while $44 million (about K77 billion) was for the land project and another $8.5 million (about K15 billion) was for a project called American Catalyst Facility for Development.

a6644.t:
Care Malawi humanitarian assistance programmes manager Burnnet Khulumbo says the flood trigger statement and anticipatory action plan will help to avert the impact of disasters in Nsanje and Chikwawa districts.
He said this on Tuesday in Chikwawa when the organisation hosted a two-day technical workshop to finalise the flood trigger statement and anticipatory action plan for the two districts.
Khulumbo said the initiative seeks to enable partners to take proactive steps ahead of predicted hazards, preventing or reducing acute humanitarian impacts before they fully unfold.
He said: “Floods remain one of the most recurrent and devastating hazards in Malawi, particularly in the Shire Valley. Therefore, this workshop will review and validate the flood trigger statement, which specifies the forecast thresholds that will activate anticipatory actions.”
Department of Disaster Management Affairs principal disaster preparedness officer Zione Viyazyi said there are no major gaps currently but there is need for more localised forecasting capacity to trigger area-specific early actions for councils such as Nsanje, Chikwawa and Phalombe.
“We have made a good progress at the national level in piloting and integrating anticipatory action into disaster risk reduction efforts. A National Anticipatory Action Framework was drafted to institutionalise the anticipatory action into national policy,” she said.
On his part, Churches Aid in Relief and Development (Card) resilience officer Michael Mwale said it was time the country moved from preparing for disasters at the higher level to involving the grassroots.
“We expect this workshop to help stakeholders finalise a trigger statement and action plan ready for operationalisation,” he said.
Care Malawi in conjunction with Card and Eagles Relief and Development is implementing Anticipatory Humanitarian Action Facility Project with funding from WeltHungerHlife.
Card is implementing the project in Nsanje while Eagles Relief and Development is running it in Chikwawa.

a6657.t:
Une trentaine de professionnels renforcent leur capacité
La mise en oeuvre du projet « Accès au foncier » du Millenium Challenge Account (Mca) Bénin suit son court. A la suite de la formation de 50 professionnels du secteur public et privé organisée du 13 au 15 mai dernier à Lokossa, il s’agit cette fois-ci pour le Mca-Bénin de former une trentaine de techniciens professionnels dont des géomètres experts du secteur public et privé à l’utilisation des stations permanentes et des récepteurs mobiles dans les domaines de la cartographie et du cadastre en vue d’atteindre les objectifs du projet « Accès au foncier ».
Pendant cinq jours, les participants vont se familiariser avec les activités topo-foncières en s’appuyant sur les 7 stations permanentes installées au Bénin grâce aux récepteurs mobiles acquises pour la réalisation des travaux topographiques avec la technologie CORS/GNSS qui est une innovation au Bénin. L’atelier de formation sera animé pour la circonstance par le Mcc, le Mca-Bénin, le ministère de l’urbanisme et celui de la défense assurera la conduite intellectuelle. Trois consultants internationaux, tous experts dans le domaine du cadastre à savoir Grenville Barnes, Walter Volkmann et Johan Bonne ingénieur photogrammètre, ont été recrutés par le Mcc à cet effet. C’est le Cta bimyns à Djrègbé qui abrite cet atelier de formation. Dans son mot de bienvenue, Bio Baguiri Seydou directeur du projet « Accès au foncier » représentant le coordonnateur empêché, a précisé qu’à travers ces installations, il entend renforcer les capacités géodésiques, topographiques et cartographiques de notre pays en le dotant d’instruments modernes de lutte contre l’insécurité foncière. Il n’a pas manqué de présenter les améliorations techniques qui seront apportées au processus d’établissement des plans fonciers ruraux (Pfr) ainsi qu’au processus de transformation des permis d’habiter (Ph) en titres fonciers (Tf). Ainsi, clarifie t-il que avec les Gps les mesures réalisées sur le terrain connaissent désormais une correction différentielle en post traitement pour augmenter la précision des mesures effectuées par les récepteurs mobiles. Selon ses explications, l’objectif du Mca-Bénin à travers le projet « Accès au foncier » est de mettre un terme aux multiples systèmes utilisés jusque là et d’avoir un seul système de référence dans notre pays. Pour finir, il dira que pendant les quatre jours, les participants vont participer à l’acquisition de données aériennes par un drone téléguidé, à s’approprier les techniques de détermination de points de contrôle de qualité des ortho images et enfin participer aux travaux de groupe sur des thématiques à des fins géodésiques, cartographiques et cadastres. Quant au directeur adjoint résident du Millenium Challenge Corporation Randy Wood, il est revenu sur les objectifs du projet « Accès au foncier », qui dans sa mise en oeuvre a prévu la réalisation de 300 titres de plans fonciers ruraux dans une quarantaine de communes rurales du Bénin ainsi que la transformation de 30.000 présumés titres de propriété en titres fonciers. L’appui et la collaboration du gouvernement béninois n’ont pas été occultés dans ses propos. Pour finir, il a exhorté les participants à suivre avec attention les différents modules qui seront présentés et qui donneront lieu à des questions d’éclaircissement. Dans son mot d’ouverture, le directeur adjoint de cabinet du ministère de l’urbanisme Didier Sacramento, cet atelier vient régler les nombreux problèmes liés à la gestion du foncier dans notre pays. Il a exhorté les participants à accorder beaucoup plus davantage à cette formation afin de trouver les solutions adéquates aux problèmes du foncier. L’attente du gouvernement c’est de voir le plus grand nombre de spécialistes formés dans l’utilisation des stations permanentes et des récepteurs mobiles dans les domaines de la cartographie et du cadastre.
Il faut préciser qu’avant le démarrage de cette formation à Djrègbé, les participants sont descendus le lundi dernier sur le terrain et plus précisément à Vagnon dans la commune d’Avrankou. Après la collecte des données, les participants traiteront ces données et les trois équipes constituées vont confronter les résultats obtenus sur le terrain. Il serait prévu également d’autres descentes sur le terrain, notamment à Adjohoun dans la vallée de l’Ouémé afin d’habituer les participants à ces appareils. Les travaux se poursuivent ce jour à travers une autre descente sur le terrain.
Ismail Kèko
a6657.en:
Use of permanent stations under the "Access to Land" project

Some thirty professionals build their capacity

Implementation of the "Access to Land" project of the Millennium Challenge Account (MCA) Benin is proceeding. Following the training of 50 public- and private-sector professionals held from 13 to 15 May in Lokossa, this time MCA-Benin is training some thirty professional technicians, including expert surveyors from the public and private sectors, in the use of permanent stations and mobile receivers in the fields of mapping and the land registry, in order to achieve the objectives of the "Access to Land" project.

For five days the participants will familiarise themselves with topographic and land activities, drawing on the 7 permanent stations installed in Benin thanks to the mobile receivers acquired for carrying out topographic work with CORS/GNSS technology, which is an innovation in Benin. The training workshop will be run for the occasion by the MCC, MCA-Benin and the Ministry of Urban Planning, and the Ministry of Defence will provide the intellectual leadership. Three international consultants, all experts in the field of the land registry, namely Grenville Barnes, Walter Volkmann and Johan Bonne, a photogrammetric engineer, were recruited by the MCC for this purpose. It is the CTA Bimyns in Djregbe that is hosting this training workshop. In his welcoming remarks, Bio Baguiri Seydou, director of the "Access to Land" project, representing the coordinator who was unable to attend, stated that through these installations he intends to strengthen the geodetic, topographic and cartographic capacities of our country by equipping it with modern instruments to combat land insecurity. He also presented the technical improvements that will be made to the process of establishing rural land plans (PFR) as well as to the process of converting occupancy permits (PH) into land titles (TF). He thus clarified that with GPS, measurements taken in the field now undergo differential correction in post-processing to increase the precision of the measurements made by the mobile receivers. According to his explanations, MCA-Benin's objective through the "Access to Land" project is to put an end to the multiple systems used until now and to have a single reference system in our country. Finally, he said that during the four days the participants will take part in the acquisition of aerial data by a remote-controlled drone, learn the techniques for determining quality control points for ortho-images and, lastly, take part in group work on themes for geodetic, cartographic and cadastral purposes. As for the deputy resident director of the Millennium Challenge Corporation, Randy Wood, he returned to the objectives of the "Access to Land" project, whose implementation provides for the production of 300 rural land plan titles in some forty rural communes of Benin as well as the conversion of 30,000 presumed ownership documents into land titles. The support and collaboration of the Beninese government were not left out of his remarks. Finally, he urged the participants to follow attentively the various modules that will be presented and that will give rise to questions for clarification. In his opening remarks, the deputy chief of staff of the Ministry of Urban Planning, Didier Sacramento, said this workshop comes to settle the many problems linked to land management in our country. He urged the participants to give much more attention to this training in order to find adequate solutions to land problems. The government's expectation is to see the largest possible number of specialists trained in the use of permanent stations and mobile receivers in the fields of mapping and the land registry.

It should be noted that before this training began in Djregbe, the participants went into the field last Monday, more specifically to Vagnon in the commune of Avrankou. After collecting the data, the participants will process it and the three teams formed will compare the results obtained in the field. Other field trips are also planned, notably to Adjohoun in the Oueme valley, in order to accustom the participants to these devices. The work continues today with another field trip.

Ismail Keko

a6951.t:
NEW YORK: THE Vice President of the United Republic of Tanzania, Dr. Philip Mpango, has said Tanzania emphasizes the importance of sustainable financing mechanisms to ensure resilience in responding to public health emergencies in Africa.
The Vice President said this while participating in the Africa Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) Heads of State and Government Committee Meeting held on the sidelines of the 80th Session of the United Nations General Assembly in New York, United States.
He said Tanzania is determined to increase domestic resource mobilization, strengthen innovative financing solutions, as well as support regional initiatives that reduce dependence on foreign aid, thereby ensuring that Africa’s health priorities are addressed by African governments.
In addition, the Vice President said domestic production of diagnostic equipment, treatment, and other essential medical products is essential for self-reliance in the health sector.
“Tanzania encourages investment in local industries, a common regulatory authority across the continent, and technology transfer partnerships to strengthen Africa’s capacity to respond to current and future health challenges.
He said recent experiences with infectious disease outbreaks, including Marburg and other infectious pathogens, have highlighted the need for strong preparedness and response systems.

“Tanzania supports the development of infectious disease treatment units, rapid deployment of emergency teams, and investment in human and health infrastructure.
He also stressed the importance of strengthening all pillars of public health emergencies, including disease surveillance, laboratories, infection control, equipment, and coordination for timely and effective response to outbreaks.
He called for enhanced cooperation among African Union Member States, regional economic communities, and the Africa Centers for Disease Control to have a unified approach to responding to health emergencies.
He said collaboration on research, policy, and joint capacity building plans will strengthen the collective ability to prevent, detect, and respond to emerging health threats.
The Committee meeting aimed to discuss issues related to the Africa Center for Disease Control (Africa CDC), under the theme ‘Ensuring Health Independence in Africa: Political Leadership for Sustainable Financing of the Health Sector, Domestic Production and Preparedness for disease outbreaks.

a6975.t:
La Guinée fait partie des pays les plus durement touchés par le démantèlement partiel de l’Agence des États-Unis pour le développement international (USAID), une mesure décidée sous l’impulsion de l’administration Trump. Selon les données officielles publiées sur le site USAspending.gov, 100 % des projets financés par l’USAID en Guinée pour l’année 2025 ont été annulés.
En tout, 12 projets, représentant 30,76 millions de dollars d’aides, ont été totalement supprimés. Ce retrait brutal frappe de plein fouet des secteurs sensibles, où ces financements américains jouaient un rôle de levier vital : santé, éducation, agriculture, gouvernance locale.
Cette décision s’inscrit dans un mouvement plus large de réduction drastique de l’aide américaine au développement, amorcé depuis le début de l’année 2025.
Selon Franceinfo et Jeune Afrique, des dizaines de pays dans le monde, notamment en Afrique, subissent des coupes sévères. Mais seuls quelques pays, dont la Guinée, voient l’ensemble de leurs financements totalement supprimés.
a6975.en:
Guinea is among the countries hardest hit by the partial dismantling of the United States Agency for International Development (USAID), a measure decided at the instigation of the Trump administration. According to official data published on the USAspending.gov website, 100% of USAID-funded projects in Guinea for the year 2025 have been cancelled.

In all, 12 projects, representing 30.76 million dollars in aid, have been completely eliminated. This abrupt withdrawal strikes hard at sensitive sectors where this American funding played a vital leveraging role: health, education, agriculture, local governance.

This decision is part of a broader movement of drastic reduction in American development aid, begun since the start of 2025.

According to Franceinfo and Jeune Afrique, dozens of countries around the world, notably in Africa, are undergoing severe cuts. But only a few countries, including Guinea, see all of their funding completely eliminated.

a6977.t:
The UN General Assembly will vote Wednesday on a draft resolution that seeks an immediate ceasefire in Gaza, a symbolic gesture after the US previously vetoed a similar action in the UN Security Council.
In addition to calling for “an immediate, unconditional and permanent ceasefire,” the draft resolution seeks “the immediate and unconditional release of all hostages,” an accommodation of the United States and other staunch allies of Israel.
The resolution, which is non-binding, also demands “immediate access” to widespread humanitarian aid for the citizens of Gaza, who have been subjected to more than a year of war with Israel, especially in the besieged north of the territory.
The war in Gaza was sparked by Hamas’s October 7, 2023 attack which resulted in the deaths of 1,208 people, mostly civilians, according to an AFP tally based on official data. The count includes hostages who died or were killed while being held in Gaza.
During the attack, militants also kidnapped 251 hostages, 96 of whom remain in Gaza, including 34 who the military says are dead.
Israel’s retaliatory offensive in Gaza has killed at least 44,786 people, mostly civilians, according to data from the Hamas-run health ministry that is considered reliable by the UN.
‘Bleeding heart of Palestine’
“Gaza today is the bleeding heart of Palestine,” Palestinian UN ambassador Riyad Mansour said last week during the Assembly’s first debate on the resolution.
“The images of our children burning in tents, with no food in their bellies and no hopes and no horizon for the future, and after having endured pain and loss for more than a year, should haunt the conscience of the world and prompt action to end this nightmare,” he continued, calling for an end to the “impunity.’
Israel, meanwhile, has denounced the draft resolution ahead of the vote.
“If you truly want peace, it begins with dismantling this infrastructure of hate and the glorification of terror,” Israeli UN ambassador Danny Danon said, in reference to humanitarian agency UNRWA, whose employees were accused by Israel of assisting with the October 7 attacks.
The draft resolution seeks to address “the need for accountability” by asking UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres to present “proposals on how the United Nations could help to advance accountability.”
An earlier draft seen by AFP aimed to establish an international mechanism to help investigate and prosecute those who are responsible for violating international law against the Palestinians. But that language was not included in the draft resolution that will be put to a vote.
A second draft resolution up for a vote on Wednesday will call on Israel to respect the mandate of UNRWA and allow it to continue its “safe and unhindered humanitarian assistance” operations, after Israel voted to ban it.
The ban, which is due to take effect on January 28, sparked global condemnation, including from key Israeli backer the United States.

a7140.t:
By Olivia Le Poidevin
 Saturday March 22, 2025
A doctor examines a malnourished baby at the Save the Children stabilisation ward in Maiduguri, Nigeria November 30, 2016. Picture taken November 30, 2016. Purchase Licensing Rights
The United Nations children's agency said on Friday it will run out of its supply of lifesaving food to treat children suffering from acute forms of malnutrition in Ethiopia and Nigeria within the next two months due to lack of funding exacerbated by Trump administration cuts to foreign aid.
Some 1.3 million children under five suffering from severe acute malnutrition risk losing access to lifesaving support this year in Ethiopia and Nigeria, UNICEF says.
In Nigeria, UNICEF said it may run out of supplies to feed 80,000 malnourished children as soon as the end of this month. Van der Heijden described recently being in a hospital in Maiduguri with a child who was so malnourished that her skin was falling off.
International donors have in recent years reduced contributions to UN agencies, including UNICEF. Its funding woes were accelerated when the United States, its top donor, imposed a 90-day pause on all U.S. foreign aid on the first day of President Donald Trump's return to the White House in January.
That action, and ensuing orders halting many programmes of the U.S. Agency for International Development worldwide, have jeopardised the delivery of lifesaving food and medical aid, throwing into chaos global humanitarian relief efforts.
"This funding crisis will become a child survival crisis," warned Van der Heijden, adding that the sudden nature of the cuts did not give the agency the ability to mitigate the risks.
Funding cuts have also hit health programmes offering nutrition and malaria care for pregnant women and children in Ethiopia. Twenty-three mobile health clinics were taken out of operation in the region of Afar, with only seven left operating due to funding cuts, according to UNICEF.
Reporting by Olivia Le Poidevin Editing by Bill Berkrot

a7385.t:
When the directive came from the US to immediately halt all research work, Dr Leila Mansoor, a senior scientist associated with a project in KwaZulu-Natal, had to make an ethical decision.
Mansoor said:
Mansoor is involved with Caprisa, an international HIV/Aids research programme alongside the University of KwaZulu-Natal.
She manages the Matrix project, where clinical trials were being conducted using a silicone ring to prevent pregnancy and HIV infection at Vulindlela Clinic in Mafakathini.
The clinical trials are one of dozens of research projects in South Africa and globally that have been brought to a standstill by the decision of President Donald Trump's administration to halt all work funded or co-funded by USAID for 90 days.
"Our participants are now very confused; we have built a relationship of trust with our communities over the years. How do we explain that the decision is based not on science but on politics?"
READ: Donald Trump's plans cause havoc and panic everywhere
This study is the third in the Matrix project. The first studies have been completed, but now they are not allowed to finalise the data analysis and provide feedback to participants and the scientific community. "Everything is now up in the air," Mansoor says.
Besides funding Caprisa, USAID has also helped finance major research projects of the South African Medical Research Council (SAMRC).
USAID allocated $45 million (nearly R829 million) in 2023 for the Brilliant Consortium, a research programme of various African countries aiming to develop a vaccine against HIV/AIDS.
Some of South Africa's internationally recognised scientists, like Professor Linda-Gail Bekker from the Desmond Tutu HIV Centre at the University of Cape Town and Prof. Glenda Gray, former head of the SAMRC, are involved in this project.
"The Brilliant Consortium, led by the SAMRC received formal communication from USAID that our work is halted until further notice," says Tendani Tsedu, SAMRC spokesperson.
American funding also supports the research work of the Desmond Tutu Tuberculosis (TB) Centre at Stellenbosch University and projects at the University of the Witwatersrand.
According to a post on USAID Southern Africa's Facebook page, they have already invested $94 million (around R1.7 billion) in TB programmes run in South Africa.
"Ten years of work will go to waste if our programmes (on HIV/Aids and TB, among others) have to pause for a few months," says another academic.
He speaks anonymously, fearing it might jeopardise their chances for funding after the three-month deadline. "It will take us years to catch up again."
He also points out the international contribution of researchers from South Africa. "Some of the most important research work on Covid-19 came from South Africa."
Thanks to the country's supply of world-class researchers, experience in HIV/Aids research, and facilities like laboratories, we were able to test vaccines and medicines for Covid-19.
"The Americans might think they don't benefit directly (from research on diseases like HIV/Aids and TB), but some diseases more common in developing countries also appear elsewhere," the academic says.
For instance, Kansas is currently experiencing one of the largest TB outbreaks ever recorded in the US, reports The Guardian, with 384 patients being monitored and treated there.
According to the researcher, South Africans must find other ways to help finance their work, but it would have made a huge difference if the process occurred in phases.
Yet another researcher points to the ethical dilemma they are facing. "You cannot just stop programmes; there are ethical guidelines and contracts on how to work with participants and scientific data, for example."
